implementation_notes:
TypeScript types the JavaScript enhancer: a generic function from component type to component type (patterns.dev writes the shape as HOC

= (Wrapped: ComponentType

) => ComponentType

) whose result is a function component rendering the wrapped component with merged props - a custom hook replaces it for new function-component logic, while the enhancer remains the tool for library APIs that must wrap any component shape. Preserving the wrapped component's contract is the type-level work: keep props generic (P extends object), strip injected props with Omit where callers must not supply them, and accept that a generic enhancer cannot preserve the wrapped component's own type parameters; refs need forwardRef (or ref-as-an-ordinary-prop on React 19+) and statics need hoist-non-react-statics.
pitfalls: A generic enhancer erases the wrapped component's own type parameters: withAnalytics<Props>(PricePanel<string>) cannot preserve the type argument, and the call site silently loses inference.
Injected props must be removed from the public props (Omit<P, keyof Injected>); leaving them in makes a collision silent instead of a compile-time error.

Refs and statics are not part of ComponentType

, so forwardRef and hoist-non-react-statics are still required - a wrapper typed as ComponentType

hides that they are missing.

variants.name: Class-container HOC (wrapper class, class-era React)
variants.idiom_name: class WithX extends React.Component { render() { return <Wrapped {...this.props} /> } }
variants.implementation_notes: The shape the React documentation itself uses (withSubscription, logProps): the enhancer returns a class container that owns the concern's state and lifecycle - componentDidMount/componentWillUnmount for subscriptions - and renders the wrapped component with merged props. Bind this variant when the wrapped units are class components or the codebase predates hooks: a hook cannot be called inside a class component, so an enhancer is the only way to share logic into one, and lifecycle-based enhancements naturally live here too. For new function-component code the props-proxy variant, and ultimately a custom hook, is the better default.
pitfalls: Lifecycle code is duplicated per enhancer; two class containers compose only by nesting, so the order of their mount/unmount behaviour is fixed by the wrapper chain.
The container's props are typed separately from the injected state, so a collision between an injected prop and a parent prop is resolved by spread order rather than by the compiler.
Class containers keep the codebase on two paradigms: use them only where class components or lifecycle-based enhancements require it.
